justification: The answer sits in the paired-grid sentence: “Both numbers moved, and they moved together: in the cold the foot stopped dead in two-thirds of the distance the warm floor needed, and slid less doing so.” That is exactly C — same drop, shorter stopping distance, less slide — the “same drop” guaranteed by “released from a fixed height” and by his reading “a grid at seven … and the same grid again at four.” A fails on “It reports two numbers – how sharply the surface stops the foot, and how far the foot slides before it stops”: both quantities are recorded, not one. B fails on the apparatus description “a weighted steel foot on a rail, released from a fixed height, with an accelerometer bolted inside it” — the rail and the fixed height are what remove hand-release variation, so it is the flat negation of the method. D is the deliberate inversion of Pallenmoor’s own comparison, “The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test”: the within-school seasonal gap is the wider one, not the between-arena gap.

The coring result is stated numerically: “Pallenmoor cored the bed in eleven places. In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3,” which is D, and the mechanism paragraph confirms the reading — “Harrowing lifts fibre … so the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one.” A is contradicted directly by “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.” B is contradicted by “The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them.” C is the most seductive competitor because the tines really did stop short (“The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130”), but it reverses the finding: “Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on” — the unturned layer was hard, not loose, and hoofprints demonstrably did reach it.

The comparison class is set up as “In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move, whatever their age,” and the causal attribution is supplied two paragraphs on: “The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work … Below about six degrees the coating is stiff … Above about twenty-five it goes slack.” Absence of the temperature-sensitive coating is therefore what leaves the damp schools reading the same morning and afternoon — B. A dies on the same sentence twice over: “some of them older than this one” and the explicit age control “whatever their age.” C misreads the very phrase that defines the class — they are laid on “plain sand and fibre,” so fibre is present, and in any case it is the wax, not fibre, that stiffens below six degrees. D contradicts “the morning grid and the afternoon grid,” which are the same two hours he used at this school (“at seven … again at four”); the readings do straddle the day and simply fail to move.

The writer’s own evaluative voice appears in “Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him” and closes the paragraph with “That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are” — she endorses precisely the limits he draws round his figures, which is A. B is refuted by his stated grounds for the one association he will make: it is “not with any surface but with change … and he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures,” so it is expressly not settled by his readings. C is refuted both by “it is worth more than they are” and by the final paragraph, where the yard acts on exactly what he found — heaters on a timer and “The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres.” D inverts the article: the riders’ report that “the school changes under them: hard and slippery for a January lesson, deep and tiring by a July afternoon” is the thing his instrument confirms, so she doubts neither, and it is the yard’s blaming of “the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor” that gets corrected.

The article isolates two live variables and eliminates the rest. Temperature: “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is”, with the paraffin mechanism at six and twenty-five degrees. Tine depth: “The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130 … the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one.” Everything else is ruled out — sand (“The sand itself had hardly changed”), wax condition (“in better condition than the wax at the top”), age (“whatever their age”) — and the yard’s fix is exactly those two: heaters to eight degrees and “The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres.” That is C. B was weighed seriously, since the timer does bring the school “above eight degrees”, but heating only addresses the cold end of the curve; “Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep” means a heated February still will not ride like a July afternoon, so B overreaches. A invents damage and end-of-life for a bed whose sand and wax both test sound. D is the direct negation of “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is.”

The gap joins two parallel observations about signal-free unanimity: the onset (“it starts everywhere at once … two hundred people find the same half-second”) and the offset (“the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal”). The word “again” marks the second clause as an additive parallel, which is exactly what sentence-initial “Equally” does in British usage — ‘likewise, and just as strikingly’. A fails on polarity of relation: “Hence” asserts consequence, but a unanimous ending does not follow from a unanimous beginning; the sentence offers a second instance, not a deduction. B fails because “Rather” requires a correction or replacement of what precedes, and nothing in the first sentences is being withdrawn — the onset claim stands. D fails on sense: “Elsewhere” relocates to other places, whereas the ending being described is the ending of this same hall’s same burst of clapping.

The collocation is fixed: applause is something a room ‘joins in’, and the clause “the room may not ___ in, and for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for” needs a verb meaning ‘add itself to what you have started’ — join in. The next sentence confirms the sense: “that is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first,” i.e. someone else joining. B, “cut in”, means to interrupt or break into something already running, the wrong direction entirely, since the risk is that nothing follows you. D, “break in”, carries the same interruptive sense plus a forced-entry reading, and would make the room the interrupter rather than the joiner. C, “fall in”, is the drill-square idiom for forming ranks on command, which both misfits the register and contradicts the paragraph’s premise that “No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch”.

The gap must name an unfolding process, not its outcome: “the coming-down is a ___ about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words.” Both “conducted” and the preposition “about” select ‘negotiation’ — negotiations are conducted, and are conducted about a question. C, “bargain”, and D, “settlement”, are both terminal nouns: they name the agreement arrived at, so they cannot be “conducted” and cannot be the “coming-down” itself, which is described as still in progress and resolving over a few seconds. A, “transaction”, implies an exchange of considerations between parties and does not take “about” in this way; nothing is being traded here, and “a transaction about how long is decent” is not English. Only B satisfies collocation, complementation and the process/outcome polarity together.

“Although X, it is not permitted to run long” is concessive, so X must be something that would otherwise justify running long — warmth, not coldness. “Wholehearted” supplies that contrast and matches what the hall gives a child performer, set against the hard four-or-five-second ceiling in the next sentence. A, “grudging”, and C, “muted”, both destroy the concession: grudging or muted applause is exactly the kind you would expect to be short, so “although” becomes incoherent. B, “outspoken”, is a category error — it describes people or statements that voice opinions plainly, not the sound a hall makes, and applause has no propositional content to be outspoken about. The paragraph’s closing image of the boy who “went on clapping long after the hall had finished” confirms that the warmth is real and the limit is social, not affective.

The clause turns on a contrast the reader is asked to hear: “A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one ___, and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder got.” Since the sound is audibly inferior to the spontaneous applause, the adverb must mark compliance without warmth — “dutifully”, applause given because it was asked for. C, “instinctively”, contradicts the framing directly: the room was “asked”, and the whole paragraph is headed “The mechanism shows itself when it slips”, i.e. these are the cases where the automatic process is absent. D, “generously”, has the wrong polarity outright — generous applause would sound like, or better than, what the recorder got. A, “narrowly”, does not collocate with giving applause at all; it would need a scalar object (narrowly avoided, narrowly won), and ‘give a hand narrowly’ is not English.

The accelerometer week is reported as “Between stations the trace barely moved” followed by her verdict “It’s the stop at the far end that does it” — the deceleration at arrival, not the transit, is what bursts the cells and drives the potassium up, which is D. A misassigns the cause of the improvement: “The loop runs at the speed it always has. What changed is the bins: two are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half” — the fall in rejects came from padding the landing, and the speed was never altered. B is refuted by “Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning”, together with the opening image of her holding “a spun tube to the window” — haemolysis is only visible once the sample is centrifuged in the lab. C reverses the one explicit exception in the piece: “Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.”

The two extents are described in matching terms, and that match is the buried point of the piece: Ruddiforth’s attorney “claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane”, while “The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the stone gap to the lane end” — same bank, same two termini, with the survey preceding the November claim, which is D (and explains the February offer “to leave the timber and keep the ground”, since compensation would follow the ground). A reverses the source of the plan: “The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan.” B fails on arithmetic: “both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839” and the letters begin in “November 1845”, six years, not a generation — and the hedge was in continuous joint use, “cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other”. C is contradicted by “The scheme was given up in the autumn of 1846, and no land was taken”, after which “In 1851 the thorn was laid again by both farms together.”

Skribentens tes står i klartext i det femte stycket: “Ändå ska den bäras. Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda”, och medgivandet om spelet står direkt före: “Textremsan låser repliken … den som vet att remsan går spelar inte som förut. Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den.” Det är precis A:s tes-plus-medgivande. B är den närmaste konkurrenten men fälls av en enda mening: “Ett svepskäl är det inte. Kostnaden är verklig och ska räknas med.” C motsägs av “Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte. Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta, och den som hör dåligt får ändå rätta sig efter någon annans kalender”, och även av “Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova.” D motsägs av “Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte … något förslag för den scenen har jag inte” — lilla scenen är uttryckligen undantagen, inte förstasteg.

Andra stycket beskriver slingan och dess användning: “Salongen har en hörselslinga, och den gör vad den ska. Man ställer hörapparaten i T-läge, och därmed är saken klar – ingen mottagare att hämta i foajén, ingen kö vid vaktmästeriet.” Det är D. A motsägs av “den gör vad den ska” i presens, och av att skribentens klagomål genomgående gäller vad slingan inte kan föra fram, inte att den slutat fungera: “Det slingan för fram är ljudet.” B motsägs av “Jag har suttit på rad tre och på rad sexton och hört lika bra på båda.” C motsägs av “Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år” — det är tvärtom slingan som redan har sin självklara plats i bladet, till skillnad från textningen som trängs ihop på en egen rad.

Häststycket bär svaret: “En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik … Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven, och ett djur som trampade igenom skar upp benen på iskanten.” Samma skare som höll för en gående brast under hoven — A, och det är också skälet till att “Hästen fick stå i stallet.” B motsägs ordagrant av “mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass”. C är nära men fel i transportledet: “Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs till fots. Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med” — skidorna användes för förflyttning, inte som ersättning för draghästen. D får fel egenskap på fel tid: “Skaren är inte hal om morgonen. Den är sträv som fint grus under sulan, och blank blir den först fram på dagen” — och då är färden ändå slut.

Planeringsstycket är explicit: “Veckorna kom när de kom. Somliga år låg skaren i mitten av mars och räckte i tre veckor. Somliga år blev det fyra morgnar på hela vintern, och ett par vintrar uteblev skaren. Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan.” Beslutet kunde alltså fattas tidigast kvällen före, aldrig i förväg — B, och hälprovet i inledningen (“Ger den efter … då blir det ingen färd den morgonen”) bekräftar att beskedet ibland kom först på själva morgonen. A motsägs av nästa mening: “Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.” C förlägger arbetet till natten; texten lägger det till morgontimmarna och begränsar dem hårt: “Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över … Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt.” D vänder på skärbildningens villkor: “Vintrar då kylan håller i sig utan avbrott lämnar snön lös hela vägen ner, för den hinner inte bli våt” — obruten kyla ger ingen skare alls.
